```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
source(here::here("scripts/sampling_theory_funcs.R"))

sd <- load_tested(here::here("data/sampled_data.csv"))
cd <- read_csv(here::here("data/case_data_delta.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ba <- read_csv(here::here("data/bias_aggregate.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Formatting helpers
num <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
num_auto <- function(x) ifelse(x %% 1 == 0, num(x, 0), num(x, 1))
neg <- function(s) paste0("$", s, "$")          # signed numbers in math: a true minus sign in any locale
sgn <- function(x, d = 1) neg(sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f"), x))
span <- function(x, d = 2) paste0(num(min(x), d), "--", num(max(x), d))  # "--" becomes an en dash
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(num(x, d), "%")
sci <- function(x) {
  e <- floor(log10(x))
  sprintf("$%.1f\\times10^{%d}$", x / 10^e, e)
}
italic_n <- function(s) sub(" n=", " *n*=", s, fixed = TRUE)
site_val <- function(df, site, col) df[[col]][df$data_source == site]
```

```{r}
#| label: compute
fy <- fy_diagnostics(sd, note_strategies)
dec <- weekly_error_decomp(sd, note_strategies)
alloc <- allocation(sd, filter(note_strategies, col %in% c(
  "sample_every2", "sample_every5", "sample_first_3_cases", "sample_first_3_cases_week"
)))
starts <- map_dfr(c(2, 5, 10), ~ everyn_start_bias(sd, .x))
order1 <- arrival_order(sd, 1)
order3 <- arrival_order(sd, 3)
dow <- weekday_positivity(sd)
kap_fy <- kappa_by_facility_year(sd)
ccor <- caseload_positivity_cor(sd)
icc <- icc_facility_day(sd)
sev <- severe_annual_bias(cd)
cov_d1 <- weekly_ci_coverage(cd, "First n daily (n=1)")
agg <- aggregation_reduction(cd, ba, main_text_labels)

n_fy <- n_distinct(paste(fy$data_source, fy$site, fy$year))
med <- fy %>%
  group_by(strategy, family, size) %>%
  summarise(rho = median(rho), kappa = median(kappa), VIF = median(VIF),
            rel = 100 * median(rel_diff), M = median(M), M0 = median(M0),
            pooled_wins = sum(pooled_wins), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(match(strategy, note_strategies$label))
fam <- function(f) filter(med, family == f)
capped <- filter(med, family != "every")
kap_fac <- kap_fy %>% group_by(data_source, site) %>% summarise(k = median(kappa), .groups = "drop")
kappa_tab <- round(median(kap_fy$kappa), 2)
weekly_wins <- function(f) span(n_fy - fam(f)$pooled_wins, 0)
o3s <- filter(order3, data_source == "Sitakunda")
dec_d3 <- filter(dec, strategy == "Daily n=3")
dow_s <- filter(dow, data_source == "Sitakunda")
dow_u <- filter(dow, data_source == "Uvira")
day_min <- function(d) paste0(num(min(d$positivity), 1), "% (", d$day_full[which.min(d$positivity)], ")")
day_max <- function(d) paste0(num(max(d$positivity), 1), "% (", d$day_full[which.max(d$positivity)], ")")
alloc_val <- function(strat, site, col) alloc[[col]][alloc$strategy == strat & alloc$data_source == site]
```

claim(all(ccor$pearson > 0), "weekly positivity rose with caseload in both sites")
claim(all(capped$rho < 0), "capped designs have a negative correlation")
claim(all(capped$rel < 0), "capped designs make the pooled estimate lower")
claim(all(capped$M > capped$M0), "capped designs are above their thresholds")
claim(all(fam("every")$M < fam("every")$M0), "every n is below its threshold")
claim(max(fam("daily")$VIF) < min(fam("weekly")$VIF), "weekly n has the largest VIF")
claim(all(abs(filter(dec, family == "daily")$D) < 1e-9), "daily n has no unsampled days")
claim(max(abs(starts$design_bias_pct)) < 1, "every-n design bias is negligible")
claim(max(starts$ht_max_err) < 1e-9, "Horvitz-Thompson is unbiased under a random start")
claim(o3s$lo < 1 && o3s$hi > 1, "no within-day arrival-order effect in Sitakunda")

This technical supplement provides some theoretical results and additional simulations to try to further understand the differences between sampling schemes and analytical approaches. 

# Setup {#sec-setup}

Work within one facility and one calendar year; the catchment estimate is the sum of facility
estimates. In week $w$ there are $N_w$ suspected cases, of which $m_w$ are tested and $x_w$ are
RDT-positive. Write $f_w=m_w/N_w$ for the sampling fraction, $\hat p_w=x_w/m_w$ for observed
positivity and $p_w$ for true positivity among all $N_w$ cases. The target is the annual number of
RDT-positive cases, $Y=\sum_w N_w p_w$. As in the main text, we simulate within the RDT-tested
population, so $Y$ is known exactly. The data comprise `r n_fy` facility-years.

The two ways of turning tests into an annual count are

$$
\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}}=\sum_w N_w\,\hat p_w,
\qquad\qquad
\hat Y_{\mathrm{pooled}}=N\,\frac{\sum_w x_w}{\sum_w m_w},
$$ {#eq-estimators}

where $N=\sum_w N_w$. We write $\mathbb{E}_N[a]=\sum_w N_w a_w/N$ for the average of a weekly
quantity over weeks weighted by suspected cases, and $\mathrm{Cov}_N$ for the corresponding
covariance.

# Weekly-summed versus pooled annual estimates {#sec-weekly-pooled}

## They differ only in how weeks are weighted

Because $x_w=m_w\hat p_w$, the pooled positivity $\sum_w x_w/\sum_w m_w$ is itself an average of
the weekly positivities, weighted by tests. Writing $m_w=f_wN_w$ and subtracting the
suspected-case-weighted average gives

$$
\hat Y_{\mathrm{pooled}}-\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}}
=N\,\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_N(f,\hat p)}{\mathbb{E}_N[f]}.
$$ {#eq-diff}

This is an exact identity; across all `r nrow(fy)` strategy–facility-year combinations it
reproduced the difference between the two estimates to machine precision (largest error
`r sci(max(fy$identity_err))`). In words, the pooled estimate hands each week more suspected cases
than it had if that week was sampled above the average fraction, and fewer if below, and values each
misallocated case at that week's positivity.

## When they agree, and which is biased

- **They agree exactly when $\mathrm{Cov}_N(f,\hat p)=0$**: the sampling fraction is uncorrelated
  with positivity, weighting weeks by suspected cases. A constant sampling fraction guarantees this
  whatever the epidemiology; otherwise it depends on the data.
- **The weekly-summed estimate is unbiased** whenever the cases tested within a week are
  representative of that week. The pooled estimate needs that *and* a zero covariance between
  sampling fraction and true positivity.
- **The sign depends on the design.** Under a cap, the sampling fraction falls as caseload rises.
  In both sites weekly positivity rose with caseload (correlation
  `r num(site_val(ccor, "Sitakunda", "pearson"))` in Sitakunda,
  `r num(site_val(ccor, "Uvira", "pearson"))` in Uvira), so the pooled estimate was too low. A
  programme that tested *more* intensively during outbreaks would see the opposite.

## What weekly summing costs

Weekly summing gives low-sample weeks full weight, which costs precision. With similar
within-week variances, the variance ratio is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{Var}(\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}})}{\mathrm{Var}(\hat Y_{\mathrm{pooled}})}
=\mathbb{E}_N[f]\,\mathbb{E}_N[1/f]\ \ge\ 1,
$$ {#eq-vif}

with equality only when $f_w$ is constant. We call this the variance inflation factor (VIF). In our
data it was `r span(fam("every")$VIF)` for every *n*, `r span(fam("daily")$VIF)` for daily *n* and
`r span(fam("weekly")$VIF)` for weekly *n* (@tbl-evidence).

::: {.callout-note}
## Three situations
**Constant sampling fraction:** the two estimates are identical, so there is nothing to choose.

**Sampling fraction varies but is unrelated to positivity** (for example, driven by test stock-outs):
pooling is unbiased and more precise, so it is better. 

**Sampling fraction varies with positivity**
(any cap on tests): pooling is biased, weekly summing is unbiased but less precise, and which has the
smaller error depends on scale.
:::

## A rule of thumb

Comparing the two errors leads, after two approximations, to a threshold that does not depend on
how much the sampling fraction varies — only on how strongly it tracks positivity. Pooling has the
smaller error when the annual number of tests per facility, $M$, is below

$$
M_0^{*}=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}\kappa},
$$ {#eq-mstar}

where $\rho$ is the (suspected-case-weighted) correlation between weekly sampling fraction and
weekly positivity, a property of the design, and $\kappa$ is the between-week variance of positivity
divided by $\bar p(1-\bar p)$, a property of the epidemiology. $\kappa$ had a median of
`r num(median(kap_fy$kappa))` across facility-years (facility medians `r span(kap_fac$k)`). Because
the bias of pooling grows with the square of the programme's size and its precision advantage only
linearly, every sufficiently large programme should sum weekly estimates. Across the
`r nrow(fy)` strategy–facility-year combinations, this rule picked the same estimator as an exact
comparison `r sum(fy$pooled_wins == fy$rule_pooled)` times.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mstar
#| tbl-cap: "Annual tests per facility above which weekly summing has the smaller error."
rho_grid <- c(0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)
tab <- as.data.frame(t(c(
  paste0("$M_0^{*}$ at $\\kappa=", kappa_tab, "$ (tests per facility-year)"),
  num(1 / (rho_grid^2 * kappa_tab), 0)
)))
names(tab) <- c("Correlation $\\rho$ (magnitude)", as.character(rho_grid))
kable(tab, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
```

Capped designs had $\rho$ between `r neg(num(min(capped$rho)))` and `r neg(num(max(capped$rho)))`
and used `r span(capped$M, 0)` tests per facility-year, above their thresholds of
`r span(capped$M0, 0)`, so weekly summing had the smaller error in `r weekly_wins("daily")` of
`r n_fy` facility-years under daily *n* and `r weekly_wins("weekly")` under weekly *n*. Every *n* had
$\rho$ closer to zero (`r neg(num(min(fam("every")$rho)))` to `r neg(num(max(fam("every")$rho)))`)
and thresholds above its test volume, so pooling was marginally better. That is why the main text
found no consistent gain from weekly summing for every *n*: the median percent reduction in absolute
bias was `r neg(num(filter(agg, family == "every", data_source == "Sitakunda")$median_reduction, 1))`%
in Sitakunda, where weekly summing slightly increased the bias, and
`r neg(num(filter(agg, family == "every", data_source == "Uvira")$median_reduction, 1))`% in Uvira.

# A general decomposition of error {#sec-decomp}

## One identity

@eq-diff is an instance of a general fact. If a quantity $a$ is averaged over a selected subset of
units, with selection intensity $g$, instead of over all of them,

$$
\frac{\sum_j u_j g_j a_j}{\sum_j u_j g_j}-\frac{\sum_j u_j a_j}{\sum_j u_j}
=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_u(g,a)}{\mathbb{E}_u[g]},
$$ {#eq-lemma}

where $u_j$ are the units' weights. The error is zero exactly when selection is uncorrelated with
the outcome. Applied to weeks it gives @eq-diff; applied to days within a week, or to cases within a
day, it gives the other error terms below.

## Four sources of error

Because we recommend summing weekly estimates, the error that distinguishes one sampling scheme from
another is the error of $\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}}$. Let $\hat p_w^{\mathrm{day}}$ be the week's
positivity obtained by weighting each sampled day by its suspected cases, and $p_w^{+}$ the true
positivity on the days that were sampled. Then, exactly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}}-Y
&=\sum_w N_w\Big[\underbrace{\big(\hat p_w-\hat p_w^{\mathrm{day}}\big)}_{\text{B: between-day weighting}}
+\underbrace{\big(\hat p_w^{\mathrm{day}}-p_w^{+}\big)}_{\text{C: within-day selection}}\\
&\qquad+\underbrace{\big(p_w^{+}-p_w\big)}_{\text{D: unsampled days}}\Big].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-four}

The pooled estimate carries one more term, $\mathrm{A}=\hat Y_{\mathrm{pooled}}-\hat Y_{\mathrm{weekly}}$
from @eq-diff. The terms form a ladder. A is weighting error across weeks, which weekly summing
removes. B is the same weighting error across the days of a week, which summing daily estimates would
remove. C and D describe *which* cases were tested, and no re-weighting can remove them.

| Term | Arises when | Removed by |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| A. Cross-week weighting (pooled estimate only) | The sampling fraction varies across weeks with positivity | Summing weekly estimates |
| B. Between-day weighting | The sampling fraction varies across days within a week | Summing daily estimates |
| C. Within-day selection | Which cases are tested on a day relates to positivity | Design only |
| D. Unsampled days | Some days in a week are never tested | Design only (or coarser periods) |
| Variance | Few tests in a period | More tests, or spreading them evenly |

: What each error term means and what removes it. {#tbl-terms}

The general principle: **summing estimates at a given time scale removes weighting error at that
scale and above, but cannot remove selection error — which cases were tested — inside the period.**

# How each sampling scheme generates error {#sec-schemes}

Below, "error" means the error of the weekly-summed estimate, terms B, C and D. Term A matters only
if a single annual positivity is used.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-evidence
#| tbl-cap: "The two sites at a glance. $\\rho$, VIF and the pooled-versus-weekly gap are medians over facility-years. The error column is a single realisation summed over all weeks with at least one test. The last column counts facility-years in which the pooled estimate had the smaller mean squared error."
#| tbl-colwidths: [16, 9, 8, 13, 34, 20]
dec_wide <- dec %>%
  select(strategy, data_source, pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = data_source, values_from = pct)
med %>%
  left_join(dec_wide, by = "strategy") %>%
  transmute(
    Strategy = italic_n(strategy),
    `$\\rho$` = neg(num(rho)),
    VIF = num(VIF),
    `Pooled vs weekly (%)` = neg(num(rel, 1)),
    `Weekly-summed error, % of truth (Sitakunda / Uvira)` = paste(sgn(Sitakunda), "/", sgn(Uvira)),
    `Pooled has lower error` = paste(pooled_wins, "of", n_fy)
  ) %>%
  kable(format = "pipe", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

**Every *n* (systematic).** Tests are proportional to caseload, so the sampling fraction is nearly
constant and term A is close to zero; the pooled and weekly-summed estimates barely differ. The
weakness is quiet weeks: a week with fewer than $n$ cases may get no test at all. In Uvira's quietest
third of weeks the median number of tests was
`r num_auto(alloc_val("Every n=2", "Uvira", "quiet_median_tests"))` under $n=2$ and
`r num_auto(alloc_val("Every n=5", "Uvira", "quiet_median_tests"))` under $n=5$, and
`r pct(alloc_val("Every n=5", "Uvira", "quiet_pct_empty"))` of those weeks went untested under $n=5$
(@tbl-alloc). The every-*n* errors in @tbl-evidence reflect which cases the fixed starting point
happened to select, not systematic bias: averaged over all possible starting points the bias was at
most `r pct(max(abs(starts$design_bias_pct)), 2)` of the truth.

**First *n* per day (daily *n*).** The cap lowers the sampling fraction on busy days, so term A is
present ($\rho$ between `r neg(num(min(fam("daily")$rho)))` and `r neg(num(max(fam("daily")$rho)))`)
but weekly summing removes it. Term B, the same effect between days of a week, was small (about
`r num(mean(abs(dec_d3$B)), 0)` cases for $n=3$). Term D is zero, because every day with a case
contributes at least one test, so no week with cases goes untested. Term C is the only open
question: whether the first arrivals of the day differ from later ones. It is zero on days with $n$
or fewer cases and shrinks as $n$ grows. In Sitakunda, the one site with arrival times, there was no
evidence of such a difference within facility-days (Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio for the first three
arrivals `r num(o3s$or)`, 95% CI `r num(o3s$lo)`–`r num(o3s$hi)`). A comparison pooled across days
appears to show one (`r num(o3s$p_first, 1)`% vs `r num(o3s$p_rest, 1)`% positive), but that is
term-A-style confounding one level down: only busy, high-positivity days contribute "later" arrivals.
Weekly-summed errors were within ±`r pct(max(abs(filter(dec, family == "daily", size >= 2)$pct)), 1)`
of the truth for $n\ge2$.

**First *n* per week from a random start day (weekly *n*).** The cap is as tight as it can be — at
most $n$ tests in a week — so term A and the VIF are the largest of any scheme. The tests fall on one
or two consecutive days, so terms C and D are large, and positivity clusters within days, which adds
variance. The random start day removes day-of-week effects only in busy weeks; in quiet weeks the
scheme tests every case from the start day to the end of the week, so later weekdays are
over-represented. Under $n=3$, `r pct(alloc_val("Weekly n=3", "Uvira", "quiet_pct_empty"))` of
Uvira's quietest weeks went untested.

**All cases on one random day per week.** Every case has a one-in-seven chance of being tested, so
seven times the positives on the chosen day is an unbiased weekly count. The weekly positivity
estimate is not: it gives every weekday equal weight rather than weight by caseload, so it is biased
whenever busy weekdays differ in positivity (term D). Testing a single day also makes it very
variable.

**All cases on a fixed weekday.** The error is entirely term D and does not average out. Positivity
ranged by weekday from `r day_min(dow_s)` to `r day_max(dow_s)` in Sitakunda and from
`r day_min(dow_u)` to `r day_max(dow_u)` in Uvira. The other days are never seen, so nothing in the
data can correct it.

**Severe cases only.** Selection depends on the outcome itself: cholera causes severe dehydration,
so severe cases are more often positive. This is term C at its worst, and no analysis can remove it
without separate information on non-severe cases. It over-estimated annual incidence in Sitakunda by
`r num(site_val(sev, "Sitakunda", "lo"))`–`r num(site_val(sev, "Sitakunda", "hi"), 1)` per 10,000.

| Scheme | A: across weeks (if pooled) | B: across days | C: within a day | D: unsampled days | Fixable in analysis |
|:---------------|:----------------|:---------------|:-------------------|:-----------------------|:----------------------|
| Every *n* | Near zero | Small | Small | Frequent when weeks are quiet | Little to fix |
| Daily *n* | Yes | Small | Arrival order, if any | None | A and B |
| Weekly *n* | Largest | Yes | Arrival order, if any | Large; weekday imbalance | A only |
| Random day | Yes | None | None | Weekday caseload differences | Use 7 × positives |
| Fixed weekday | Yes | None | None | Persistent day effect | No |
| Severe only | Yes | Yes | Outcome-driven | Some | No |

: Which error terms each scheme produces. {#tbl-schemes}

# Why the daily cap works at both time scales {#sec-why}

**Annual burden** is estimated most precisely when tests are proportional to caseload, which is what
every *n* does. Under proportional allocation the two estimators coincide and there is no weighting
error.

**Weekly trends and outbreak detection** need adequate precision in *every* week, including quiet ones.
The precision of weekly positivity depends on the number of tests that week, not on the caseload:
its standard error is roughly $\sqrt{p(1-p)/m_w}$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-se
#| tbl-cap: "Approximate standard error of weekly positivity. These ignore the finite-population correction, so they overstate the error when most of a week's cases are tested."
m_grid <- c(3, 5, 10, 20, 30)
se_tab <- data.frame(
  row = c("SE at positivity 20%", "SE at positivity 50%"),
  rbind(num(sqrt(0.2 * 0.8 / m_grid)), num(sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / m_grid)))
)
names(se_tab) <- c("Tests in the week, $m_w$", m_grid)
kable(se_tab, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
```

For this target, the best use of a fixed budget is a similar number of tests every week, and
proportional allocation is the worst case, because quiet weeks get almost none. A cap on tests per
day approximates equal allocation:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-alloc
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("Tests in the busiest versus quietest third of weeks. Peak weeks had ", num(site_val(distinct(alloc, data_source, caseload_ratio), 'Sitakunda', 'caseload_ratio'), 1), " times the caseload of quiet weeks in Sitakunda and ", num(site_val(distinct(alloc, data_source, caseload_ratio), 'Uvira', 'caseload_ratio'), 1), " times in Uvira; proportional allocation would match those ratios. Where the quiet-week median is zero, the ratio uses 0.5 in its place.")
#| tbl-colwidths: [18, 14, 22, 22, 24]
alloc %>%
  arrange(match(strategy, note_strategies$label), data_source) %>%
  transmute(
    Strategy = italic_n(strategy),
    Site = data_source,
    `Tests, peak vs quiet weeks` = num(test_ratio, 1),
    `Median tests, quiet week` = num_auto(quiet_median_tests),
    `Quiet weeks with no test` = pct(quiet_pct_empty)
  ) %>%
  kable(format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The cap's cost at the annual scale is term A, which weekly summing removes at no cost in tests, plus
a VIF that is small for daily *n* (`r span(fam("daily")$VIF)`). Every *n* makes the opposite choice:
ideal for annual totals, but it starves quiet weeks. Weekly *n* makes the same choice as daily *n* at
far too low a level of testing: it pays the same cost but buys too few tests to benefit.

# Heuristics {#sec-heuristics}

| Goal | Scheme | Annual estimator | Why |
|:----------------------|:--------------------------|:---------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| Annual burden, adequate caseload | Every *n* or daily *n* | Either for every *n*; weekly sums for daily *n* | Every *n* needs no correction; daily *n*'s weighting error is removed by weekly sums |
| Weekly trends and outbreak detection | Daily *n*, $n\ge3$ | Weekly sums | Tests every week with cases, with low weekly error |
| Low or seasonal incidence | Daily *n* | Weekly sums; coarsen to fortnights or months if many weeks are thin | Every *n* with large *n* leaves quiet weeks untested |
| Very limited test supply | Daily *n* with small *n* | Weekly sums | Keeps tests spread across days and weeks; daily $n=1$ still gave weekly 95% CI coverage of `r span(cov_d1$coverage, 0)`% |

: Choosing a scheme and estimator, based on the theory above and the two study sites. {#tbl-heuristics}

1. **Match the estimator to the design.** Any cap on tests per day or week calls for summing weekly
   (or finer) estimates. Pooling one annual positivity is reasonable only under a self-weighting
   design such as every *n*, or when annual test volume is below $M_0^{*}=1/(\rho^2\kappa)$.
2. **Budget tests for the quietest weeks you care about.** Use @tbl-se to decide how many tests a week
   you need. Under every *n* a week gets about $N_w/n$ tests, so $n$ should not exceed the quiet-week
   caseload divided by that number. Under daily *n* a week gets at least one test per day with cases.
3. **Cap per day, not per week.** A daily cap spreads tests across days, never leaves a week with
   cases untested, and avoids the weekday imbalance of weekly caps.
4. **Never select on something related to the outcome.** Severity-based or fixed-weekday sampling
   produces error that no analysis can correct.
5. **Summarise at the finest period the data support.** Summing weekly estimates removes weighting
   error; where many weeks have no tests, move to fortnights or months rather than filling gaps by
   imputation.
6. **Check the two assumptions the recommended schemes rely on.** Test for differences between early
   and late arrivals *within* facility-days, never pooled across days, and record weekly
   suspected-case counts carefully, since weekly summing uses them as weights.

# Caveats {#sec-caveats}

- The evidence comes from two endemic sites and `r n_fy` facility-years.
- The precision results assume the cases tested within a week are representative of that week, and
  ignore clustering of positivity within facility-days (latent-scale intraclass correlation
  `r num(site_val(icc, "Sitakunda", "icc"), 3)` in Sitakunda and `r num(site_val(icc, "Uvira", "icc"), 3)`
  in Uvira), which makes schemes that test one or two days per week less precise than shown.
- Weeks with no tested case are excluded from these calculations; the main analysis imputes them.
- Arrival order could be examined only in Sitakunda; Uvira has no within-day arrival times.
- As in the main text, RDT misclassification is ignored.
